questions.question: Dmitri Ivanovsky passed sap from tobacco plants sick with mosaic disease through a porcelain filter in 1892. The filter's pores were fine enough to hold back bacteria, yet the clear sap that came through still made healthy plants sick. What did that result show, on its own, about the cause of the disease?
choices: It was smaller than bacteria
It was a poison that bacteria made
It could multiply inside living leaves
It was a new kind of living germ
questions.context: A cause that slips through pores which stop bacteria must be smaller than they are; viruses are now known to be about a hundredth the size of most bacteria. The filter could not say whether that tiny cause was a poison or a living thing that multiplies, and Ivanovsky himself suspected a poison made by bacteria. Martinus Beijerinck settled the question in 1898 by passing the sap from plant to plant.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology tells how viruses were found by filtering sap, and asking what one result can and cannot show on its own is the grade's core reasoning about evidence.

questions.question: Martinus Beijerinck repeated the filter test on tobacco mosaic disease, which mottles the leaves, in 1898. Then he infected a healthy plant with the filtered sap, used sap from that plant to infect another, and so on down a line of plants. The disease did not fade down the line. Why did that rule out a poison as the cause?
questions.answer: A poison would have been watered down at every step
choices: A poison would have been watered down at every step
A poison could never have passed through the filter
A poison would have killed the plants, not mottled them
A poison would have stayed in the first plant it reached
questions.context: Each plant received only a little of the sap of the one before, so a fixed dose of poison would have thinned out until the disease faded; instead the agent was multiplying inside each living plant. Dissolved poisons do pass such filters, as diphtheria toxin does, which is why the filter alone could not decide. Beijerinck found the agent would grow in no broth, only in living, growing tissue, and he named it a virus.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to judge which result would separate two explanations, and Beijerinck's line of plants is the textbook step from a filterable agent to one that reproduces.

questions.question: Wendell Stanley purified the cause of tobacco mosaic disease in 1935 into fine, needle-shaped crystals, as a pure chemical forms. Dissolved and applied to healthy leaves, the crystals still gave them the disease. Most biologists do not count a virus such as this one as a living thing. What is their main reason?
questions.answer: It can copy itself only inside a living cell
choices: It can copy itself only inside a living cell
It is a single cell, but with no nucleus
It is pure protein, with no genes inside
It never changes from one generation to the next
questions.context: A virus is genetic material, DNA or RNA, in a coat of protein, with no ribosomes or energy-making chemistry of its own: outside a cell it does nothing, and inside one it makes copies with the cell's own machinery. Stanley first took his crystals for pure protein, but they were soon found to hold RNA, and viruses do evolve, often fast. Whether they are alive is still argued, and some biologists place them at the very edge of life.
questions.grade_note: The ninth-grade standard compares viruses with cells, and why a virus is not usually counted as alive is its central question.

questions.question: A boy has a runny nose and a sore throat from a cold, and his mother asks the doctor for an antibiotic. Penicillin, one of the best known, kills bacteria by wrecking the wall that each one builds around itself as it grows. The doctor says no antibiotic can cure a cold. What is the reason?
questions.answer: A virus has none of the parts such drugs attack
choices: A virus has none of the parts such drugs attack
A virus has grown resistant to all such drugs
A virus is too small for such drugs to hit
A virus multiplies too fast for such drugs
questions.context: Antibiotics strike parts that bacteria have and human cells lack, such as the wall penicillin wrecks and the bacteria's own ribosomes. A cold virus has no wall and no ribosomes; it copies itself with the machinery of the boy's own cells, so the drug has nothing to hit. An antibiotic taken for a cold does no good and adds to the overuse that breeds resistant bacteria.
questions.grade_note: The ninth-grade standard on viruses asks students to explain why antibiotics act on bacteria and not on viruses.

questions.question: Alexander Fleming found a blue-green mould growing on a dish of staphylococcus bacteria in his London laboratory in September 1928, and the bacteria around it had been destroyed. The dish alone could not show whether the killing needed the living mould itself. Which test could answer that?
questions.answer: Test broth the mould grew in, with the mould filtered out
choices: Test broth the mould grew in, with the mould filtered out
Grow the mould alone on a fresh dish with no bacteria
Set the mould on a dish of a different kind of bacteria
Look at the dead bacteria under a far stronger microscope
questions.context: Fleming did just that: the clear, straw-coloured 'mould juice' that came through the filter still worked against staphylococci, streptococci and pneumococci, so the killer was a substance the mould gives off, not the living mould. Mould alone on a dish, or mould on new bacteria, still leaves the mould and the killing together, and a sharper look at dead cells cannot say what killed them. In March 1929 he named the substance penicillin, in place of the clumsy phrase 'mould broth filtrate'.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade investigation design asks which test isolates one variable, here the living mould against the substance it releases.

questions.question: Alexander Fleming named his mould's bacteria-killing substance penicillin in a paper of 1929. Yet for about ten years after that, almost no one used it to treat a sick person. What held it back?
questions.answer: No one could purify it before it broke down
choices: No one could purify it before it broke down
It harmed white blood cells as well as germs
It killed only bacteria that cause no disease
It sickened the animals it was injected into
questions.context: Penicillin falls apart quickly, and neither Fleming's assistants nor Harold Raistrick's team in 1932 could get it out of the mould broth pure. It did not harm white blood cells, nor the mice and rabbits Fleming injected, and it worked against staphylococci and streptococci. From 1939 Ernst Chain, Howard Florey and Norman Heatley at Oxford found how to extract and keep it, the work that the press long credited to Fleming alone.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that a discovery and a working medicine are different achievements, and penicillin's lost decade is the standard example.

questions.question: Howard Florey's team at Oxford, among them Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley, gave eight mice a deadly dose of streptococcus bacteria on 25 May 1940, then gave four of them penicillin. By the early hours of the next morning, all four untreated mice were dead and the four treated ones were alive. What did this show that Alexander Fleming's own tests had not?
questions.answer: That it could save an animal from an infection
choices: That it could save an animal from an infection
That it did an animal no harm when injected
That it could kill streptococci in a dish
That no kind of bacteria could ever resist it
questions.context: Fleming had shown that penicillin worked against streptococci in a dish and did injected mice and rabbits no harm, but he never treated an infected animal, the crucial step; the four untreated mice proved the dose of bacteria was deadly. Bacteria that destroy penicillin had been found that same year. The 1945 Nobel Prize went to Fleming, Florey and Chain, and the rule of three winners at most left Heatley out.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks what a new experiment shows beyond earlier ones, and the Oxford mouse test is the step from a dish to a cure.

questions.question: Doctors at a hospital find the same gene for resisting one antibiotic in two kinds of bacteria that are not close relatives. New mutations that give resistance are rare, at most about one cell in a million each generation, yet the gene has spread through both kinds within a few years. How did it most likely travel?
questions.answer: Bacteria passed copies of it directly to one another
choices: Bacteria passed copies of it directly to one another
The antibiotic changed both kinds' genes the same way
Both kinds inherited it from a shared ancestor
Each kind hit on the very same mutation by chance
questions.context: Bacteria can hand genes to other living bacteria, even of another species, often on plasmids, small extra loops of DNA passed from cell to cell; this sideways sharing is the main way resistance spreads. A shared ancestor would pass a gene down over ages, not across two kinds in a few years, and an antibiotic writes no genes: it only favours the cells that already carry one.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that bacteria can share genes, resistance genes among them, and this case asks students to reason from the evidence to that route.

questions.question: Vanessa D'Costa and her colleagues studied genetic material (DNA) from ground in the far north that had stayed frozen for 30,000 years, long before anyone made a medicine. Mammoth DNA in it, and none from moose or spruce, showed the DNA was ancient, not modern. Among the old genes were ones that let bacteria resist modern antibiotics, vancomycin among them. What does the find show about how antibiotics bring on resistance?
questions.answer: They favour resistance genes that already exist
choices: They favour resistance genes that already exist
They make bacteria build new genes to resist them
They make the patient's own body resist them
They breed resistance only when people misuse them
questions.context: Genes that defeat today's drugs were in the ground 30,000 years before any medicine, for soil microbes have long made antibiotics to fight one another; a drug writes no resistance genes, it kills the cells that lack them and leaves those that carry them to multiply. Every use favours them, so the find is no reason to relax: heavy use in hospitals and on farms favours these old defences all the more. The patient's body never becomes resistant; the bacteria do.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that selection acts on variation already present, and these ancient genes are direct evidence that antibiotics pick out resistance rather than create it.
